info.desc: Check Your Head is the third album by the Beastie Boys, released on April 21, 1992. Three years elapsed between the release of Paul's Boutique (the band's second album) and their recording of this album. Check Your Head was recorded at the G-Son Studios in Atwater Village, California in 1991. The album features the popular hits "So Whatcha Want" and "Pass the Mic"; the music videos for both songs are available on the Criterion Collection Beastie Boys Video Anthology DVD set. The album was re-released in 2009 in a number of formats and featured 16 b-sides and rarities as well .

podcast.body: Released after a three-year gap, this album marked a significant shift in the band's sound and approach, moving away from heavy sampling due to artistic desire and economic necessity (cost of clearing samples). Recorded at their self-built G-Sun studio in Los Angeles with Money Mark on keyboards and Mario Caldato Jr., the album solidified their musical credibility and sold well, reaching the top 10 of the US album charts. "Check Your Head not only solidified the Beastie Boys' musical credibility, it also sold big time reaching into the top 10 of the US album charts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Released on April 7, 1992, this album marked a significant shift for the band, representing their "comeback album" and solidifying their musical credibility after the commercial disappointment of their previous record. The album sold "big time, reaching into the top 10 of the US album charts." "The thinking was, they'd taken the sampling thing about as far as they could, so it was time for a different approach."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: The Beastie Boys' 1992 album *Check Your Head* features the song "Pass the Mic," which is highlighted as an excellent example of sampling technology broadening the sonic palette for alternative rock in the 1990s. The track is built from samples of at least seven different songs, showcasing complex audio construction. "The Beastie Boys, with a fine example of how sampling technology broadened the palate for the sounds of Alt Rock in the 1990s."
